articles.title: Senado aprova PEC da Segurança Pública sem texto que trata da maioridade penal  | G1
articles.standfirst: O texto aumenta a atuação do governo federal no enfrentamento do crime organizado.
articles.summary: O texto aumenta a atuação do governo federal no enfrentamento do crime organizado.
articles.body:
O Senado aprovou nesta terça-feira (3) a PEC da Segurança . O texto aumenta a atuação do governo federal no enfrentamento do crime organizado.

O relator da proposta, senador Rogério Carvalho, do PT, seguiu a orientação do governo e apresentou o mesmo texto que foi aprovado na Câmara, deixando de fora as propostas para reduzir a maioridade penal. Em outubro, a oposição anunciou que votaria a favor da PEC da Segurança, mas apresentou uma emenda para reduzir a maioridade penal para 16 anos para a maioria dos crimes e para 14 no caso de crimes hediondos - como o tráfico de drogas e homicídio. Na tentativa de diminuir o impacto da estratégia da oposição, o líder do PT no Senado, Camilo Santana, apresentou uma outra emenda com a redução da maioridade para 16 anos, mas só para crimes hediondos.

Nesta terça-feira (3), o senador Rogério Carvalho propôs que elas sejam discutidas em uma outra PEC, separadamente, em um outro momento, por entender que o tema precisa ser mais debatido. O presidente do Senado colocou em votação a retirada das emendas. Por 38 votos a 36, os senadores decidiram que o tema vai ser tratado em outro momento, em PECs separadas. Qualquer mudança no texto obrigaria a PEC da Segurança a voltar à Câmara para nova votação dos deputados. Isso adiaria os planos do presidente Lula de criar, ainda em 2026, o Ministério da Segurança Pública. Senadores falaram da importância da aprovação da PEC.

"Isso fruto do que todos nós, senadores, parlamentares, políticos, colhemos das ruas. Porque é, sem nenhuma dúvida, uma das pautas prioritárias do povo brasileiro, junto com a saúde pública e com a educação, é a segurança pública nesse país, para que o Brasil comece a dar resposta em segurança pública ao povo que está vulnerável nas ruas, nas avenidas, nas casas, nas vielas do nosso país, e nos rios do nosso país", diz o senador Eduardo Braga, MDB - AM.

Senado aprova PEC da Segurança Pública sem texto que trata da maioridade penal — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

Em seguida, os senadores aprovaram por unanimidade, em dois turnos de votação, a PEC da Segurança Pública, que agora vai à promulgação para entrar em vigor. Uma vitória do governo após as eleições.

A PEC dá mais poder ao governo federal para agir contra as organizações criminosas; permite que os bens usados em atividades criminosas sejam expropriados, sem indenização; amplia as atribuições da Polícia Federal no combate ao crime organizado e expande a atuação da Polícia Rodoviária Federal em hidrovias e ferrovias; coloca na Constituição o Sistema Único de Segurança Pública, o SUSP, que vai integrar a atuação das forças de segurança da União, estados e municípios; e permite ainda a criação de polícias municipais. Também prevê punições mais severas para os chefes de facções criminosas, que deverão cumprir pena obrigatoriamente em prisão de segurança máxima. Não poderão progredir de regime e ficam fora da chamada "saidinha". A líder do governo comemorou o resultado.

"Nós estamos criando pela, pela PEC, o Sistema Único de Segurança Pública. Nós estamos, portanto, envolvendo os três entes federados no controle, na promoção da segurança e no combate à violência. Agora com o sistema articulado, sim, nossa expectativa é muito positiva em relação a esse sistema, porque o sistema não está solto. Ele vai existir no Orçamento, ele vai existir no Ministério da Segurança, onde também vão ser tratadas as questões pertinentes ao combate efetivo ao crime organizado e às facções", diz a senadora Teresa Leitão, PT - PE.

articles.title: Alasca pode protagonizar uma das maiores derrotas de Donald Trump nas eleições | G1
articles.standfirst: Já o Texas, a principal base eleitoral do Partido Republicano e, por isso mesmo, é um dos mais importantes alvos para o Partido Democrata nessa eleição.
articles.summary: Já o Texas, a principal base eleitoral do Partido Republicano e, por isso mesmo, é um dos mais importantes alvos para o Partido Democrata nessa eleição.
articles.body:
A correspondente Carolina Cimenti foi para o Texas, que é a principal base eleitoral do Partido Republicano, e por isso mesmo é um dos mais importantes alvos para o Partido Democrata nessa eleição.

"Está animado por aqui. Olha, se em 2024 os republicanos conseguiram construir uma muralha vermelha de votos para eleger Donald Trump em vários estados, a fortaleza dessa muralha era o estado do Texas. Só que essa fortaleza republicana agora, nessas eleições, ela está em jogo. Desde 1988 os texanos não elegem um democrata para o Senado americano. Segundo as pesquisas, isso pode mudar hoje. Os texanos ainda estão votando, olha só, bastante movimento por aqui. E eles estão bastante mobilizados. Lá no oeste do estado, na região de El Paso, as urnas ainda vão ficar abertas até as 23h do horário de Brasília. Mas a gente sabe, já falou sobre isso, tudo aqui no Texas é muito grande. É a segunda maior economia dos Estados Unidos , é o estado com a segunda maior população e é o segundo estado mais importante nas eleições presidenciais. Por isso, a campanha legislativa dos candidatos democrata e republicano aqui no Texas se tornou a campanha mais cara da história dos Estados Unidos. Óbvio, os dois partidos estão de olho no que os texanos vão fazer daqui dois anos, na próxima eleição presidencial. Mas não é só esse estado de maioria republicana que os democratas estão querendo conquistar da mão do Partido Republicano. Lá no outro lado do país, um estado com uma população muito menor do que a do Texas, o Alasca, está chamando muita atenção. E as urnas por lá vão continuar abertas até as 3h do horário de Brasília", diz a correspondente Carolina Cimenti.

O Alasca não costuma estar no centro das atenções. É um estado distante, que tradicionalmente vota no Partido Republicano, mas que tem pouca expressão na política nacional, e agora pode protagonizar uma das maiores derrotas de Donald Trump nessas eleições. 95% da comida no Alasca vem de fora. Quase tudo de navio. Desde fevereiro de 2026, quando o governo Trump começou a guerra contra o Irã, o diesel ficou 70% mais caro e a conta do frete foi repassada para os consumidores.

A realidade abalou a reeleição do senador republicano Dan Sulivan, que apoia as medidas do presidente. Nas pesquisas de intenção de voto, ele aparece ligeiramente atrás da candidata democrata, Mary Peltola. Ela promete baixar o custo de vida e priorizar pescadores locais e indígenas. A pesca é um dos pilares da economia no estado.

Alasca pode protagonizar uma das maiores derrotas de Donald Trump nas eleições — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

Um terceiro candidato ao Senado também virou notícia, mas pelo nome: o mesmo do republicano que tenta a reeleição. Dan J. Sulivan é professor aposentado, mora em uma cidade de 3 mil habitantes, nunca tinha se envolvido com política e disse que se candidatou porque está insatisfeito com o governo. O Partido Republicano acusa a campanha de Mary Peltola de estar por trás da candidatura do professor para tentar confundir os eleitores.

Uma investigação do “New York Times” revelou que aliados da democrata articularam, nos bastidores, a entrada do candidato para dividir os votos que iriam para o republicano Sulivan. A candidata democrata nega qualquer envolvimento. Forrest Nabors, professor na Universidade do Alasca, explicou:

"O eleitor no Alasca pega a cédula e vê dois Dan Sulivans – um, o republicano que tenta a reeleição, e o outro, esse professor aposentado independente. Se não prestar atenção, você pode votar para o Dan Sulivan errado. E, em uma eleição apertada como esta, uma margem de erro de 3% pode determinar o resultado”.

A apuração no Alasca pode demorar até duas semanas. Esse é, de longe, o maior estado americano em território, mas com a terceira menor população, que vive espalhada em zonas remotas. Além disso, por ser no extremo norte do planeta, lá neva muito. Algumas áreas só dá para acessar de avião. Quem vota pelo correio tem até esta terça-feira (3) para enviar a cédula, que precisa chegar até um dos cinco centros de apuração. Em Anchorage, onde vivem 40% da população do Alasca, eleitores passaram mais de duas horas na fila para votar. Um eleitor afirma:

"É a chance de dizer o que acreditamos que precisa acontecer e temos que usufruir desse direito”.

articles.title: Lula comemora aprovação da PEC da Segurança Pública e reforça criação de ministério | G1
articles.standfirst: Proposta dá mais poder ao governo federal para agir contra as organizações criminosas e prevê punições mais severas para os chefes de facções criminosas. Presidente não anunciou quem vai assumir a nova pasta.
articles.summary: Proposta dá mais poder ao governo federal para agir contra as organizações criminosas e prevê punições mais severas para os chefes de facções criminosas. Presidente não anunciou quem vai assumir a nova pasta.
articles.body:
A proposta, que agora segue para promulgação, dá mais poder ao governo federal para agir contra as organizações criminosas, amplia a cooperação entre União, estados e municípios e prevê punições mais severas para os chefes de facções criminosas , que deverão cumprir pena obrigatoriamente em prisão de segurança máxima ( veja mais detalhes abaixo ).

Em uma rede social, Lula reforçou que, a partir da aprovação da PEC, vai criar o Ministério da Segurança Pública. Na postagem, o presidente não anunciou quem vai assumir a pasta.

"Vamos somar a esse avanço a criação do Ministério da Segurança Pública, com foco em inteligência, planejamento e cooperação com estados e municípios para enfrentar as facções e as milícias", escreveu Lula.

"O povo brasileiro tem o direito de trabalhar, voltar para casa e viver com tranquilidade. Garantir esse direito é um compromisso do Governo do Brasil."

O vice-presidente Geraldo Alckmin também comemorou a aprovação da PEC e disse que a partir de agora será "combate sem trégua ao crime organizado e proteção ao cidadão".

"Agora nós vamos poder atuar com firmeza no combate ao crime, junto com estados e municípios. A União vai assumir um papel maior protegendo o cidadão e colocando criminosos na cadeia. Na prática, integração entre as polícias, compartilhamento de informações, mais recursos para a segurança. Combate sem trégua ao crime organizado e proteção ao cidadão."

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) — Foto: Ricardo Stuckert

A proposta estabelece na Constituição o Sistema Único de Segurança Pública (SUSP) , cujo objetivo é integrar o combate ao crime organizado entre os entes.

De acordo com o texto, União, Estados e Distrito Federal poderão criar leis na área de segurança pública, incluindo forças-tarefa intergovernamentais, organização das polícias e guardas municipais e do sistema socioeducativo.

Outro ponto central da PEC da Segurança Pública é sobre o combate a crimes violentos e facções criminosas .

Entre as medidas estão a obrigatoriedade de prisão em estabelecimento penal de segurança máxima ou de natureza especial .

Também fica proibida ou restringida a progressão de regime, a concessão de liberdade provisória, com ou sem fiança, e de saída temporária .

A PEC também permite a expropriação de todo e qualquer bem, direito ou valor econômico envolvido com as atividades criminosas . As regras valem para organizações criminosas, paramilitares e de milícia privada.

criação de polícias municipais para o policiamento ostensivo e comunitário;

ampliação da atuação da Polícia Rodoviária Federal (PRF) para o policiamento de hidrovias e ferrovias, além de apoiar outras forças de segurança, quando requisitada pelo governador;

manter a Polícia Federal e PRF sob competência privativa da União, assim como as normas para atividades de inteligência.

Um dos nomes fortes para assumir a chefia do novo ministério é do promotor de Justiça do Grupo de Atuação Especial de Repressão ao Crime Organizado (Gaeco) de Presidente Prudente (SP), Lincoln Gakiya, conhecido pela atuação no combate ao Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC).

Dias antes do segundo turno, Gakyia participou de um jantar na casa do advogado Marco Aurélio de Carvalho, coordenador da campanha de Lula no estado de São Paulo. Durante o encontro, o promotor foi consultado sobre os principais desafios da segurança pública e compartilhou experiências no combate ao crime organizado . Mas não houve convite para que o promotor assumisse o cargo.

Segundo interlocutores do presidente Lula, o ponto a favor de Gakyia é sua biografia, por representar o combate ao crime organizado no país.

No entanto, o promotor não tem uma relação estabelecida com o presidente e teria que criar essa relação de confiança com Lula para ser uma opção real para comandar o Ministério da Segurança, o que ainda não aconteceu.

Uma outra questão é que o presidente Lula ainda não definiu nomes para ministérios do quarto mandato, o que, na avaliação desses interlocutores, pode fazer total diferença na hora do petista fazer sua escolha para a Segurança.

Os eventuais papeis de Fernando Haddad, Camilo Santana e André Fonteles no quarto mandato ainda não foram definidos.

articles.title: Trump says he could use "tremendous powers" if Democrats win
articles.summary: President Trump remained optimistic about GOP chances ahead of polls closing: "We have a good chance. But we're not going to be embarrassed."
articles.body:
"I have the ultimate power — it's called 'veto,'" President Trump told CBS News in an exclusive phone interview before polls closed across the country in this year's midterm elections , when asked about the prospect of a Democratic-controlled Congress next year.

Mr. Trump says he is prepared to veto Democratic legislation if necessary, and he welcomes the moniker "Mr. Veto," in terms of describing his approach to Democrats, should they win a majority in the House or Senate.

Pollsters have been predicting some GOP losses and in late October, CBS News' polling suggested Republicans could be on track to lose control of the House .

Still, Mr. Trump remained optimistic on Tuesday when asked about the Republican Party's chances during the phone interview. And he said that regardless of the results and the makeup of Congress next year, he feels confident about his ability to pursue his agenda in the coming two years. He remarked that recent Supreme Court decisions have empowered him and his administration to wield expansive executive powers inside the federal government even if Congress tries to block him.

In the interview, Mr. Trump cited Trump v. Slaughter, a Supreme Court decision from earlier this year that allowed him to fire Rebecca Slaughter, a member of the Federal Trade Commission, and said that 6-to-3 decision enables him to exert sweeping control over many federal agencies, boards and commissions, regardless of who holds majorities in the House and Senate.

"We won the Slaughter case and the Slaughter case gives the president tremendous powers that it never had before," Mr. Trump said.

The president said that he plans to move forward his agenda next year in numerous federal areas with this ruling as part of the foundation for his coming executive actions.

"The presidency, our presidency, is considered a strong presidency. You can do a lot," Mr. Trump said.

Mr. Trump also believes his veto power could eventually force Democrats to cut bipartisan deals with him, should they make gains.

"Historically, you veto for a couple of months and then they come and say, 'We've got to make a deal,'" Mr. Trump said.

Mr. Trump's comments signal that there will likely be a dramatic showdown between the executive branch and Congress next year, should Democrats win majorities in each respective chamber, and he asserted that he could ramp up his use of executive power if Democrats try to constrain him on Capitol Hill.

Two people close to Mr. Trump, who requested anonymity to discuss private conversations, said discussions over executive actions have taken place at the White House in recent weeks, with deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller and Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought central figures in those talks. The range of issues being considered for further executive action includes immigration and trade, the people said.

One person close to the president said that "while Democrats may win power," Mr. Trump will "keep the power to do almost everything he wants" next year on trade, the border, managing the federal government and handling U.S. foreign policy and national security.

Regarding the midterm elections , Mr. Trump said he believes he did everything he could to help Republicans across the country in recent weeks, and said his efforts helped to recast the elections as a possible blue wave into something more competitive.

"If you remember, about 30, 40 days ago, people were saying it's going to be a big loss, and now people are talking about, like we could even win it," Mr. Trump said. "I think the tour made a big difference. I did 29 days, 33 of these things, and they were all massive rallies, they were big rallies. No one has ever done anything like it. And I think we got the word out. I think we got the enthusiasm out, too."

When asked about his motivation for his extensive tour of campaign stops, Mr. Trump said, "I just think that we're doing so well that I didn't want to see anything get in the way of what we've done," and he argued that the passage of last year's One Big Beautiful Bill Act and his efforts on trade are driving growth in different economic sectors.

The president did not make any firm predictions about Tuesday's outcome.

"We'll have to see," Mr. Trump said, noting that most Election Days come with surprises and unforeseen developments. "Will we win? We have a good chance. But we're not going to be embarrassed."

Mr. Trump spent part of Monday delivering a speech in front of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C., where he talked at length about his push to renovate, clean or rebuild key structures at the White House and around the capital.

In the Tuesday interview, Mr. Trump said his speech was part of his desire to show the American people that he is using skills as a lifelong developer to redevelop Washington for their use.

"Obama criticized me," Mr. Trump said, referring to former President Barack Obama's criticism of Mr. Trump's activity. "But we had broken windows by the front door" at the White House, he said, and "it was such a sad thing to look at."

"It's the White House," Mr. Trump said. "You can't have an area where the stone is cracked and half-falling off the side of the wall. And I fixed it. You know, I'm very good at that."

"I actually enjoy doing it," Mr. Trump said. "A lot of people, that doesn't relax them, it makes them crazy, but with me, it relaxes me because I really do it well, and the White House is now pristine."

When asked about what his focus is for 2027, in terms of renovations in and around Washington, the president said he expects to finish the new ballroom at the White House and to begin work on his proposed 250-foot arch, which has faced legal challenges.

"I'll be finishing that," Mr. Trump said of the ballroom. "It's a ballroom and military complex." As for the arch, "We hopefully will be starting that."

"It's a celebration of success," Mr. Trump said of the planned arch.

"I do that stuff, it's fun for me, but it's important," Mr. Trump said of his many building initiatives, and he framed his projects as a larger attempt to spruce up the country.

"We had 97 places where we had 'S-G,' which means 'serious graffiti,'" Mr. Trump said of his administration's cleanup of Washington, D.C. "Ninety-seven places, like at the base of the Supreme Court."

As for his own political future, Mr. Trump said he is not yet talking with his advisers about pursuing a potential 2028 campaign, which would face steep constitutional and legal hurdles, and, for now, said the GOP has a "very good bench" of possible candidates.

articles.title: Redução da maioridade penal: Senado faz acordo para votar PEC | G1
articles.standfirst: Pedido do líder do MDB, Eduardo Braga, tenta acelerar votação sobre o tema, depois de PEC da Segurança ser aprovada sem essa emenda. Expectativa de parte dos líderes é de votar o texto nesta quarta.
articles.summary: Lideranças do Senado fecharam acordo para votar a redução da maioridade penal nesta semana, com propostas que variam entre 14 e 16 anos para crimes hediondos.
articles.body:
Líderes do Senado fecharam um acordo nesta terça-feira (3) para que a redução da maioridade penal tenha sua votação acelerada. A expectativa de parte dos líderes é de votar o texto no plenário já nesta quarta-feira (4).

O acordo foi fechado em meio à votação da Proposta de Emenda à Constituição (PEC) da Segurança Pública . A aprovação sem o tema era um pedido do governo, que defendia uma discussão mais aprofundada sobre o tema .

O presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), chegou a defender o envio do tema com rapidez para a Comissão de Constituição e Justiça (CCJ), mas o líder do MDB, senador Eduardo Braga (AM), discordou. Para ele, o tema precisa ser votado rapidamente, de preferência ainda nesta semana .

Segundo ele, o acordo entre os líderes do PT, Camilo Santana (CE) e do PL, Carlos Portinho (RJ) no Senado, pode permitir acelerar a votação.

"A minha sugestão - que falei ainda há pouco com o senador Camilo e com o senador Carlos Portinho - é de que amanhã, aqui no Plenário, nós apresentássemos um requerimento de urgência e de quebra de interstício para que nós pudéssemos votar, aqui no plenário do Senado, a PEC de autoria do senador Camilo Santana, que estabelece maioridade penal a partir de 16 anos para crimes hediondos, que me parece que constrói o entendimento", disse Braga.

Portinho defendeu que, depois de o calendário especial ser aprovado, os senadores votem em dois turnos a redução da maioridade penal. Ainda assim, ele reconhece que ainda não há acordo sobre qual texto deve ser votado.

➡️A proposta do PL é para a maioridade penal diminuir para 16 anos em casos de crimes de menor gravidade, e para 14 anos nos hediondos.

➡️A proposta do PT reduz a maioridade para 16 anos apenas para crimes hediondos, mantendo para os demais.

"Ambas as propostas convergem na redução da maioridade penal. E isso é um grande avanço", disse Portinho. "Então a gente vai defender sim que chegue aos 14 anos, mas temos a satisfação de saber que o governo resolveu admitir a redução da maioridade penal, de alguma forma".

Já a líder do governo no Senado, Teresa Leitão (PT-PE), disse que é preciso aguardar o que virá realmente como proposta para que se saiba quais serão as condições de votar ou não a redução da maioridade penal nesta quarta.

"É um debate que precisa ser feito, mas é um debate que precisa considerar muitas variáveis. É um debate que não pode ser feito de afogadilho, é um debate que tem relação com constitucionalidades também", disse a líder do governo. "E se a gente vai enfrentar esse debate, tem que enfrentar com a segurança que ele requer".

Plenário do Senado Federal durante sessão deliberativa ordinária — Foto: Waldemir Barreto/Agência Senado

A votação da redução da maioridade penal foi adiada nesta terça-feira (3) depois de o relator da PEC da Segurança Pública, senador Rogério Carvalho (PT-SE), conseguir aprovar um pedido para que as duas emendas sobre o tema se tornassem PECs separadas .

Inicialmente, a ideia era de que os textos fossem encaminhados para a CCJ, discutidos na comissão e só depois votados em plenário. Havia ainda a possibilidade de esperar a aprovação da PEC que já está em discussão na Câmara dos Deputados.

A redução para 16 anos em casos de crime hediondo foi defendida pelo presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) durante a campanha presidencial. O PL, no entanto, quer reduzir a idade para punição penal para 14 anos.

articles.title: Michigan live results: 2026 Senate election
articles.summary: Michiganders on Tuesday will pick their next U.S. senator to serve for a six-year term, with two-term incumbent Sen. Gary Peters (D) opting not to seek reele...
articles.body:
Michiganders on Tuesday will pick their next U.S. senator to serve for a six-year term, with two-term incumbent Sen. Gary Peters (D) opting not to seek reelection.

The Michigan race is perhaps one of the most high-profile midterm contests this year, taking place in a state President Trump won in two out of his three presidential campaigns, including 2024. The Wolverine State was eyed by Republicans as a potential flip opportunity early in the cycle, and the nomination of public health official Abdul El-Sayed made them even more optimistic.

El-Sayed, who led the health departments in Detroit and Wayne County in the last decade, very narrowly won the nomination earlier this year over more moderate U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens in a contentious and closely watched race. State Sen. Mallory McMorrow also ran in the primary and, at one point, led in some polls, but she dropped out before the election.

On the Republican side, former Rep. Mike Rogers is mounting a second bid for the upper chamber, after previously having fallen short two years ago against now-Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who was at the time a member of the U.S. House.

Polls close at 8 p.m. or 9 p.m. EST, depending on location within the state.

articles.title: Chris Pappas will be the first out gay man in the U.S. Senate
articles.summary: Pappas’ win in New Hampshire makes LGBTQ+ history and protects a vulnerable seat for Democrats.
articles.body:
In New Hampshire, Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas defeated former Sen. John Sununu, a Republican backed by President Donald Trump, according to projections by Decision Desk HQ. Pappas will be the first out gay man to serve in the upper chamber.

This race, which had no incumbent, is one of a handful of competitive elections that will determine which party ultimately takes control of the Senate. Pappas' win protects a vulnerable seat for Democrats, who need to gain four seats to clinch a majority.

Pappas' win marks only the third time in history that an out LGBTQ+ person has been elected to the Senate. The first was Sen. Tammy Baldwin of Wisconsin, who took office in 2013. The second was former senator Kyrsten Sinema, a Democrat-turned independent from Arizona. Laphonza Butler, the country's first Black lesbian senator, was not elected: California Gov. Gavin Newsom appointed her to the position in 2023 for a 14-month term.

Pappas' identity as a gay man was not central to his campaign, but he didn't shy away from sharing his life with voters, either. In his campaign announcement video, while promising voters that he can help get the country "back on track," Pappas and his husband hold hands and share a loving look.

Pappas previously represented New Hampshire's 1st Congressional District for four terms, from 2019 until this year. Before that, he served two terms in the state House of Representatives.

Pappas is known as a moderate Democrat who takes a bipartisan approach to politics: While in Congress, he frequently broke with his party on House votes . But he has consistently earned top ratings from Reproductive Freedom for All , an abortion rights group, and AFL-CIO , the nation's largest federation of unions. As a co-chair for the Congressional Equality Caucus, which advocates for LGBTQ+ rights in Congress, Pappas has been a lead sponsor for major pro-LGBTQ+ bills.

Pappas entered the race after Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen did not seek reelection, leaving the seat open. In the primary, he defeated progressive challenger and democratic socialist Karishma Manzur.

He outraised Sununu by over $15 million, according to Open Secrets , which tracks money in politics. Both candidates received millions in out-of-state funds.

Pappas was endorsed by former Vice President Kamala Harris, as well as figures across the aisle like Don Bolduc, the 2022 Republican nominee for U.S. Senate in New Hampshire, and former GOP state Sen. Rick Russman. Those endorsements signal a willingness among some Republicans to break with the party as led by President Donald Trump.

Sununu, who served in the U.S. Senate from 2003 to 2009, attempted to distance himself from Trump later in the election. He released an ad in late October saying he had "never even met the man" and pledging opposition to the president's policies if they hurt people in New Hampshire.

Both men campaigned on using their past experiences in Congress to address issues like healthcare, affordability and protecting Social Security.

On the campaign trail, Sununu did not mention Pappas' identity as a gay man — giving voters a rare moment of civility during a midterms cycle characterized by name-calling and overtly cruel personal attacks in races across the country.

articles.title: What motivated voters in the 2026 midterm elections, according to The AP Voter Poll
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — Republicans in Tuesday’s midterm races were hoping their candidates could hold onto the winning coalition that President Donald Trump assem...
articles.body:
APTOPIX Election 2026 America Votes Kansas

WASHINGTON (AP) — Republicans in Tuesday's midterm races were hoping their candidates could hold onto the winning coalition that President Donald Trump assembled in the 2024 presidential election, but The AP Voter Poll suggests the GOP has lost ground with multiple key groups.

The poll, an expansive survey of about 80,000 voters in all 50 states, suggests young voters were less likely to back House Republicans this year than they were to support Trump in 2024. Young voters — those under 30 — were also more likely than older voters to say their vote for the U.S. House was cast to express opposition to Trump, and Hispanic voters were also less likely to support Republican candidates than Trump two years ago.

Most voters say the economy or the state of democracy is the top issue facing the country, with the cost of living and government corruption weighing heavily on many Americans' minds as they cast a ballot in Tuesday's midterm elections. The poll also signals a strong desire for Congress to take a more forceful role in checking the presidency.

But the survey also found that while Democrats have at least a slight advantage on several major issues, including the economy and government corruption, the Democratic Party is not much more popular among U.S. voters than the Republican Party.

Young voters and Hispanic voters appear to shift away from Republicans

After moving toward Trump in the 2024 election, young voters appear to have swung away from the Republican Party in this year's midterms.

The AP Voter Poll shows about 7 in 10 voters under 30 nationally say they supported the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race, while about 3 in 10 say they voted for the Republican. That's a shift from 2024, when the youngest voters were roughly split between Trump and Vice President Kamala Harris.

Young voters make up a fairly small share of voters. Only about 1 in 10 voters in the 2026 midterms are under 30, which limits the impact of the shift.

But their displeasure with the country and its leadership is clear: About half of young voters say they are "angry" about the way things were going in the country today, compared with about one-third of voters ages 65 and older.

The survey also suggests Republicans may have lost the ground Trump gained with Hispanic voters in 2024, though to a lesser extent than with younger voters.

Only about one-third of Hispanic voters say they backed the Republican in their local U.S. House race, while roughly 4 in 10 voted for Trump two years ago. About 6 in 10 Hispanic voters nationally say they voted for the Democratic candidate in their local House race.

About 7 in 10 Hispanic voters say Trump's policies have worsened economic conditions in the U.S.

Many voters were driven by opposition to Trump

While Trump was not on the ballot, many voters had him on their minds.

The AP Voter Poll finds about 4 in 10 voters report wanting "to express opposition" to Trump with their vote for Congress. Just under 2 in 10 voters wanted "to express support" for the president, and roughly 4 in 10 say Trump was not a factor in their decision.

Most young voters — those under 30 — said their vote was cast to express opposition to Trump. Older voters, who tend to be more conservative in general, were less likely to say they were trying to signal their dissatisfaction with the president.

The survey highlighted voters' unhappiness with Trump's leadership. About 6 in 10 disapprove of how he's handling the presidency. Views of Trump's priorities were also mostly negative. About 6 in 10 voters say Trump places a higher priority on his personal interests than the country's interests.

Voters think Congress isn't doing enough to check an unpopular president

Most voters nationally want to see Congress provide more checks and balances on the presidency, and they overwhelmingly disapprove of how Congress is handling its job.

The survey suggests voters want to see Congress take on a stronger role as a co-equal branch of government. Roughly 7 in 10 voters say Congress is doing "not enough" to provide checks and balances on the presidency. Only about 2 in 10 say it's doing "about the right amount," and about 1 in 10 say Congress is doing "too much."

That dissatisfaction with Congress's role wasn't confined to Democrats, the poll found: The vast majority of independents and about 4 in 10 Republicans say Congress is not doing enough.

The survey reflects deep unhappiness with the president and Congress. About 6 in 10 voters disapprove of how Trump is handling the presidency, while about three-quarters of voters disapprove of the way Congress is handling its job.

Concerns about democracy and corruption rival the economy for voters

The economy was a clear concern for voters, who expressed alarm over the high cost of gasoline and food.

But the survey found many voters are also deeply worried about the state of democracy and government corruption.

About 4 in 10 voters say the economy is the top issue facing the country, and roughly 3 in 10 say the state of democracy is the top issue. Only about 1 in 10 say the same about immigration or healthcare, and few named foreign policy or crime.

Roughly half of U.S. voters said government corruption and the cost of living were "crucial" to their vote for Congress, higher than the share that said that about immigration enforcement policies, the war in Iran or AI data centers.

Most voters who said government corruption was "crucial" for their vote for Congress supported the Democratic candidate for the U.S. House, while about 4 in 10 said they voted for the Republican. About 8 in 10 voters who said "the state of democracy" was the top issue facing the country supported the Democrat, while about 2 in 10 supported the Republican.

Democrats have an an advantage on handling issues

Democrats have at least a small advantage in their perceived handling of several major issues, although a significant share of voters say they don't trust either party.

Voters are slightly more likely to say Democrats would handle the economy and government corruption better than Republicans, two issues that emerged as highly important to voters in this election. Democrats also have a small edge on foreign policy and a wider advantage on their handling of transgender issues and healthcare. Voters split on which party would better handle artificial intelligence and taxes, while Republicans have a small advantage on immigration.

Despite Democrats' relative advantage on issues, though, the Democratic Party is not much more popular with voters than the Republicans. Just under half of voters have a "somewhat" or "strongly" favorable view of the Democratic Party, while about 4 in 10 view the GOP positively.

The AP Voter Poll is a survey of the American electorate conducted by SSRS for The Associated Press, ABC News, CBS News, CNN, FOX News Media, NBC News and Versant. The survey blends probability-based and non probability-based interviews with registered voters in all 50 states conducted from Oct. 19 to Nov. 3 in Alaska and Oct. 22 to Nov. 3 in all other states. A detailed methodology statement is available here . The margin of sampling error is plus or minus 0.6 percentage points for the full sample.

articles.title: Bennett ousts Kean Jr. in battleground New Jersey House race
articles.summary: Former healthcare executive Rebecca Bennett will defeat Rep. Tom Kean Jr. (R) in New Jersey’s 7th Congressional District, capitalizing on what many Democrats...
articles.body:
Former healthcare executive Rebecca Bennett will defeat Rep. Tom Kean Jr. (R) in New Jersey's 7th Congressional District, capitalizing on what many Democrats viewed as a key flip opportunity, Decision Desk HQ projects .

Bennett led Kean 60.3 percent to 38.3 percent with 76 percent of the vote reported, according to DDHQ as of 9:46 p.m. EST Tuesday.

The race was already seen as a strong pickup opportunity for Democrats, as President Trump carried the district by only 2 percentage points in 2024. But the race received much more attention and the incumbent garnered significant scrutiny over his months-long absence from the Capitol without explanation.

Kean's absence began in March, and he didn't return to Washington until the end of June. His office for months didn't provide details of his situation and only indicated he was dealing with a health issue and would return soon. Kean's GOP colleagues said they weren't sure where he was or what he was dealing with.

The congressman eventually returned after an absence of four months, revealing he was being treated for depression. He said his doctors recommended he stay in the hospital, and what he believed would not be a long-term stay grew longer.

Kean's explanation cleared up the confusion but not the scrutiny, as critics took issue with the significant amount of time that he spent away without any explanation given to his constituents.

Bennett, a former Navy helicopter pilot, didn't focus much on Kean's absence during the campaign, instead focusing on affordability concerns and tying the incumbent to the unpopular president.

Kean is the scion of a longtime New Jersey political family and the son of former Gov. Thomas Kean (R), who led the state in the 1980s. He flipped the seat in 2022 and narrowly won reelection in 2024 but fell short in his bid for a third term.

articles.title: Trump-endorsed Republican Byron Donalds becomes Florida’s first Black governor
articles.summary: Donalds, who billed campaign as ‘a continuation of the DeSantis-era of success’, becomes state’s first black governor
articles.body:
Republican Byron Donalds will be the next governor of Florida, and its first Black leader, after defeating Democrat David Jolly in one of the country's most-watched midterm races.

Donalds was endorsed by Donald Trump and appeared twice with the president at rallies in the campaign's closing days despite previously appearing to distance himself . He will succeed Ron DeSantis, the former presidential candidate who will be termed out of office in January.

Both parties portrayed the race as pivotal after eight years of DeSantis's leadership, and sent heavyweight names to Florida to bolster their candidates.

Trump shared a platform with Donalds at rallies in Fort Myers and Daytona Beach, despite the president's nationwide unpopularity over the Iran war and the cost of living threatening to cut into previously solid Republican support that saw him win the state three times.

Those campaigning for Jolly included Bill Clinton, the former president who also headlined a fundraiser that brought in $3m for his campaign. Barack Obama also gave Jolly his endorsement.

Central to both parties' argument to voters was the legacy of DeSantis, who spent good chunks of his governorship on culture war issues, including assaults on the LGBTQ+ community, reshaping higher education, and enforcing Trump's harsh second-term immigration crackdown.

Donalds touted the outgoing governor's endorsement and billed his campaign as "a continuation of the DeSantis-era of success", while warning that Jolly was seeking "to undo what Ron DeSantis built".

Jolly, pointing to the high cost of living in Florida, including soaring housing and property insurance costs, did not disagree.

"I'll fight to lower costs, and always put you first," was Jolly's final pitch to voters in television and social media advertising last week.

The new governor inherits a divided state where a booming economy and population growth has driven up costs and forced many people to leave . Almost 70% of respondents in a September poll cited economic pressures and housing affordability as their top concern.

Another significant factor in the direction Florida will take under its new leadership will be the makeup of the state legislature, where a Republican supermajority in recent years acted as an effective rubber stamp for almost every DeSantis initiative.

The Republican House and Senate leaders have, however, signaled a desire to become more independent.

articles.title: Will Epstein files be a top priority for Democrats after midterm wins?
articles.summary: Midterm voters had several issues on their minds, with the release of information surrounding the Epstein investigation among them.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Voters heading to the polls had several issues on their minds, with the release of information surrounding the Jeffrey Epstein investigation among them.

The investigation — and collections of documents widely known as the Epstein files — has remained a contentious issue across the political spectrum since President Donald Trump took office in January 2025.

The case, spanning more than two decades, has kept the Justice Department at the center of efforts to unseal a large collection of court records identifying dozens of the disgraced financier's associates.

Epstein files accountability will be on winning Democrats' list: Chris Cuomo

As for Democrats, they have been calling for accountability with the files after another allegation was made Tuesday. One unnamed Democrat told NewsNation's Chris Cuomo that will happen if the party is victorious in the midterms.

"That is going to be a focus for us," the Democrat told Cuomo. "The American people demand it, and it's the right thing to do. So that is going to be on the agenda."

NewsNation's Leland Vittert added that the incoming election results suggest voters are motivated by more than just affordability concerns, pointing to corruption as another key issue driving their decisions.

"Democratic consultants found that any time they could tie a Republican candidate to an Epstein issue, it was extraordinarily successful for them in focus groups," he said. "Now, say whatever you want about the issue, what it means, but unquestionably, Democrats viewed that and have used that throughout this campaign."

Cuomo noted that a Democratic victory could present its own challenges, arguing that the party would be expected to confront any allegations that arise rather than ignore them while in power.

"Again, what got the Democrats here will not get them where they want to be in the next cycle," he said. "So they talked a lot about Epstein. Let's see what they do about it."

Dems win could turn Epstein issue into political distraction: Katie Pavlich

Katie Pavlich argued that if Democrats win, it will be interesting to see whether they are willing to investigate members of their own party.

"It's not quite a Republican issue, but you know, you want to go investigate Barack Obama's former White House counsel, who was deeply involved in the Epstein situation," she said.

"But I think if they will find accountability on that issue, it might come too close to the party when they're trying to get other issues done. And it could turn into a political distraction for them, as it turned into the Republicans."

Mike Nellis, a former senior adviser to Kamala Harris, pushed back on Pavlich's remarks, arguing that the Epstein case serves as a gateway to broader concerns about corruption in Washington.

"Everything that Donald Trump has done in the last two years has been about enriching himself and protecting a very small, powerful group of people," Nellis said. "What Katie just said is right: There are a lot of Democrats that are in the Epstein files to prosecute all of them. I would encourage my party to be aggressive in that."

articles.title: Biden’s revenge: His alumni are winning in the midterms
articles.summary: The former president wasn’t a prominent force on the trail, but some of his one-time staffers have won high profile races on Tuesday night.
articles.body:
Joe Biden was unceremoniously ushered out of the White House two years ago.

On Tuesday, he got a small measure of revenge.

Prominent Biden administration alumni are winning in a handful of notable races, with Keisha Lance Bottoms — the one-time Atlanta mayor turned Biden's senior adviser and director of the Office of Public Engagement — leading the pack by flipping Georgia's governorship.

The victories, his former staffers say, are an important part of rehabilitating his legacy within a Democratic Party that all but banished him in 2024.

"It's proof that President Biden assembled a talented team of public servants — who the public is calling on now to help turn this country around," said Ron Klain, Biden's former chief of staff. "These fantastic men and women will make life more affordable, health care more available, protect our rights, fight corruption, and make our country stronger."

Biden was not a regular on the trail this year, and most Democrats kept their distance from the former president. But he did weigh in on a handful of primaries, helping put loyal lieutenants in front of voters who still held him in high regard.

While Bottoms was the highest profile victory, there's a number of Biden alumni also poised to head to Washington. Gabe Amo, who won a 2023 special election in a blue Rhode Island seat, secured his second full term in Congress. And Dan Koh, who won Massachusetts' 6th District to succeed Rep. Seth Moulton, was Biden's deputy Cabinet secretary and deputy director of the White House Office of Intergovernmental Affairs.

He leaned into his Biden endorsement throughout the campaign and this week reposted a video of a phone call he and his family had with Joe and Jill Biden on primary night in September.

"Mr. President and Madame first lady, thank you so much for all of your support," he told them. "It wouldn't have been possible without both of you. … You changed my life by giving me a job of a lifetime. And you got my back the minute I decided to run."

Biden's Cabinet also had a strong night in other governor races. Xavier Becerra, Biden's secretary of Health and Human Services, had a solid polling lead over Republican Steve Hilton in the race to be California's next governor going into Tuesday. And, Deb Haaland, Biden's Interior secretary, was projected to win the New Mexico governor race.

"In his farewell speech, President Biden warned that 'an oligarchy is taking shape in America of extreme wealth, power, and influence that literally threatens our entire democracy,'" said Andrew Bates, the former president's longtime spokesperson. "He urged his team and supporters to keep standing up for the values that we all care about, including decency, hard work, and a sense of national community. On the ballot and off, a whole lot of his alumni are fighting to carry on that legacy."

CORRECTION: A previous version of this report misstated how many full terms Gabe Amo has served.
authors: Alex Gangitano, Sophia Cai and Lisa Kashinsky

articles.title: A blue wave, a rejection of Trump and other takeaways from the midterms
articles.summary: The Democratic wave is here. The party claimed control of Congress and won governors’ races across the country on Tuesday – and now, as votes are counted in...
articles.body:
The Democratic wave is here . The party claimed control of Congress and won governors' races across the country on Tuesday – and now, as votes are counted in more key states, the question is how many more Republicans will be wiped out.

Across the political map , the blue shift has been enormous. In rural Middle America, the huge margins of victory that Donald Trump posted two years ago have plummeted. In heavily Latino congressional districts, the president's 2024 gains have evaporated.

And though the White House is already deflecting blame, Trump's interventions in his party's attempts to hold its House and Senate majorities seem to have only hurt the GOP's chances.

Trump's recruiting efforts and endorsements were backfiring. Candidates he'd backed over other prominent Republicans had lost or were trailing in Senate races in North Carolina, Georgia, Texas and South Carolina. His redistricting gambit also appears to have fallen flat. In Florida, Democrats won several districts that were redrawn to guarantee Republican victories.

In Texas, long the country's biggest red state, Democrats are in contention to break their decadeslong lockout from statewide office — not just in the high-profile Senate race, but also potentially in the gubernatorial contest and other statewide races.

Millions of votes remain to be counted, and it's far too early to know the full implications of Tuesday's elections. What's clear already, though, is that Americans broadly rejected Trump — and Democrats stand to make huge gains because of it.

Democrats flip six Senate seats — and aim for more

Democrats have already flipped six Republican-held Senate seats the party needed to claim the majority, winning races in Texas, Ohio, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina and South Carolina — and doing so by defeating several candidates who were hand-picked by Trump.

State Rep. James Talarico ushered in a generational moment for Texas Democrats as he defeated Ken Paxton, the scandal-plagued Republican state attorney general who was endorsed by Trump, in what became the most expensive Senate race in US history.

In Iowa, state lawmaker Josh Turek defeated Rep. Ashley Hinson — one of the GOP's star recruits of the 2026 cycle — in the race to replace retiring Republican Sen. Joni Ernst. Turek made the case that the state was bearing the brunt of Trump's tariffs and high diesel prices resulting from the war with Iran.

In Ohio, two years after losing the state's other Senate seat, Democrat Sherrod Brown completed a political comeback by defeating Republican Sen. Jon Husted.

In Kansas, megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton defeated Republican Sen. Roger Marshall — the latest reminder that though it's barn red at the presidential level, voters in the state are willing to elect Democrats.

In North Carolina, former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper trounced former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley — an outcome that was widely expected by strategists in both parties.

South Carolina, though, was a stunner. Democrat Annie Andrews defeated Darline Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham — claiming a seat that's been in GOP hands since Strom Thurmond switched parties in 1964. A Democrat hasn't won a Senate race in the Palmetto State since 1998.

A roster of South Carolina political veterans had been interested in running for the seat after Lindsey Graham's death in July. But Trump asked Graham's sister — a political novice — first to occupy the seat temporarily and later pressured her to run for a full term. She struggled in debates and on the campaign trail.

South Carolina was nowhere near the top of the Democrats' list of the most winnable GOP-held seats. And a victory there is a good sign for the party's chances in states that were expected to be more competitive — including Maine, Iowa and Alaska.

Further buoying the Democrats' hopes of a Senate majority was an early, decisive win by Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff. The race was another example of Trump's failed midterm maneuvering: His endorsement boosted Rep. Mike Collins to a primary win over a more moderate alternative backed by popular two-term Republican Gov. Brian Kemp. Ossoff's strengths and Collins' struggles helped Democrats win the governor's race in Georgia, as well, with Keisha Lance Bottoms now set to become the nation's first Black female governor.

Florida House races showcase Dem momentum and offer signs of a big Latino swing

In Florida, the results offered evidence of a potentially enormous swing among Latino voters in Democrats' favor.

Democrats held onto three seats that Republicans had redrawn in an effort to guarantee victories this fall. CNN has projected that Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz will win in redrawn districts, as will Democrat Pia Dandiya in the 22nd District.

In another heavily Hispanic district in central Florida the GOP had redrawn, Democratic Rep. Darren Soto narrowly leads his Republican challenger in the 9th District.

But the biggest eye-opener might come in South Florida's 27th District, which is based in the overwhelmingly Latino Miami-Dade County.

Republican Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar released a buzzy ad this year standing in front of the White House, criticizing Trump's immigration policy. She won by 20 percentage points two years ago. She might hold on this year — but she leads Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez by just over a thousand votes. But a swing of that size means the gains Trump made with Latino voters in 2024 have effectively evaporated, at least in Florida.

Trump drags down Republicans, but appears unlikely to accept the blame

Trump watched returns come in from the White House East Room, where the mood was described as tense. Notably, he went silent on Truth Social for three hours Tuesday night as Democrats kept winning races before posting just after 10:30 p.m.: "I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP."

Left unsaid was that Trump had spent weeks telling his supporters to pretend he was on the ballot — and that he hand-selected many of the candidates who have been suffering tonight. Candidate weakness in South Carolina, North Carolina and Texas in particular became a major headache for national Republicans, who were forced to spend millions contesting races they never expected to be close.

Officials have stressed that Trump "left it on the field" — doing what he could to retain congressional majorities but also seeding the ground to pin any Republican losses on the candidates themselves.

Trump has been aware that he was likely to catch blame if Republicans lose. That was part of his rationale for carrying out a frenetic campaign blitz over the last month, which by his own admission was exhausting. He says he tried to cut it short, but was convinced to hold final events in Iowa and Kansas. "We gave this a very strong shot," Trump said Monday at his Reflecting Pool speech, acknowledging history was not on his side.

The results were full of encouraging signs for Democrats who may want to run for president in 2028.

At least two potential White House contenders, Govs. JB Pritzker of Illinois and Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, cruised to victory in their reelection bids. Pritzker nodded to speculation about his political future in his victory speech, saying he's been asked, "What's next?"

"The answer is simple: I'm going to ask you to continue to hope, to wrap yourself in hope, in courage," Pritzker said. "We climbed one mountain tonight, but we are sitting at the base of another."

Another possible White House contender, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, was not on the ballot Tuesday but scored a big win when his former aide, Zach Dembo, flipped a GOP-friendly House district in central Kentucky.

And in Georgia, Ossoff's decisive victory is likely to increase 2028 buzz surrounding him, even if he has denied interest in running. Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms winning the governor's race means a fellow Democrat could pick his replacement in the Senate if he were to vacate his seat for a presidential run.

This story has been updated with additional details.

articles.title: James Talarico wins Texas Senate race in a massive flip for Democrats
articles.summary: The 37-year-old state legislator will be the first Democrat that the Lone Star State has sent to the upper chamber of Congress since 1988
articles.body:
Democrat James Talarico shook the national political landscape Nov. 3 by defeating Republican Ken Paxton for U.S. Senate in deep red Texas, becoming the first Democrat to win that seat since 1988, according to projections from Decision Desk HQ and NBC News.

His win is one of the most significant flips in modern history after nearly a decade-long attempt by Democrats to win a Senate seat. The 37-year-old state legislator's victory also puts the powerhouse Texas, which holds 40 electoral votes, the second most in the country behind California, in play ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

In the lead up to the Nov. 3 election, Talarico had a hold of a coveted voting bloc: Latino voters . Hispanic voters account for more than a third of Texas' electorate, the second largest portion of any state behind New Mexico.

For years, Democrats hoped that Texas could be in play as the state grew more diverse. Charismatic Democratic Senate nominees, such as Beto O'Rourke in 2018, raised hopes of turning the state blue on the back of the Latino vote, only to see those hopes consistently dashed on Election Day.

But a majority of Hispanic voters in Texas, who had previously backed Democrats, voted for President Donald Trump in 2024. Trump won 55% of the Latino vote in the state, a 13-percentage-point increase from 2020, a record high for a Republican presidential candidate and a 27-percentage-point increase over 2016, according to data from the Texas Politics Project .

The Latino swing back towards Democrats powered the party's surge in 2026.

See Dem. Texas State Rep. James Talarico as he campaigns for US Senate

Talarico framed much of his campaign around a more populist-aligned economic message that urged Texans to stop looking at traditional liberal and conservative labels. Instead, he focused his message on fighting the super-wealthy, including Elon Musk , the world's richest person, who spent millions in favor of Paxton.

"Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars. He wants his very own personal United States senator," Talarico said during an October rally in San Antonio.

articles.title: Democrat Amy Acton Defeats Vivek Ramaswamy in Ohio Governor’s Race
articles.summary: A divisive attack ad drew bipartisan condemnation before Acton’s victory delivered a significant blow to Republicans in Ohio.
articles.body:
Dr. Amy Acton will be Ohio's next governor, defeating her Republican opponent Vivek Ramaswamy in a heated race that has gained national attention in recent weeks over a controversial attack-ad against the Democrat.

On Tuesday evening, AP called the race for Acton, who previously served as the director of the state's health department during the COVID-19 pandemic, reporting that she won 50.8% of the vote with 86% of votes counted. Ramaswamy, who was backed by President Donald Trump, earned 45.9% of the vote, according to AP.

Acton's victory marks the first time in two decades that Ohioans have elected a Democrat to the governorship. It represents a significant blow to Republicans, who initially liked their chances in a state that the President won by double digits in the 2024 election.

Ramaswamy attack ad sparks widespread controversy

The race, which was an open battle since current Republican Gov. Mike DeWine was restricted from running again because of term limits, took a striking turn in the lead-up to Election Day. The Cook Political Report had previously rated the race as "Lean Republican," but later adjusted its analysis and marked it a "Toss Up." On Oct. 23, though, the Cook Political Report shifted the race slightly in Democrats' favor to "Lean Democrat."

The election forecaster attributed its latest assessment in part to an attack ad released by Ramaswamy's campaign in October. The ad featured Acton's estranged mother, who lost custody of Acton and her brother in 1978, the same year that their stepfather was indicted on charges of raping Acton when she was a child.

It sparked backlash across the political aisle. Acton's brother, Philip Stearns, described the ad as "a despicable low."

"It's not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother's husband into a political talking point," Stearns said in a statement . "This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core—a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants."

The state's current Republican governor said that the ad was "deeply, deeply troubling" and "just plain wrong," calling for Ramaswamy's campaign to rescind it. DeWine maintained, nonetheless, that he still endorsed Ramaswamy and "the whole [Republican] ticket."

But Ramaswamy, who launched an unsuccessful bid for the Republican nomination in the 2024 election, doubled down on the ad. Both Trump and Vice President J.D. Vance defended him in the wake of the outrage.

articles.title: Trump explodes at Fox News for midterm elections coverage
articles.summary: Trump targeted the network's coverage of the polling results and took shots at one of its show hosts.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — President Donald Trump lashed out several times at Fox News on Tuesday for their coverage of the midterm elections .

Trump criticized the outlet's polling results and claimed the network has given ample airtime to Democrats, who are projected to be the majority party in the both the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate , according to NewsNation's election partner Decision Desk HQ.

DDHQ projected Democrats would take control of both chambers as of 11:30 p.m. ET on Tuesday.

"The Fox News Poll, always the worst, is so insulting with the questions they ask. Every question is a hit job, and every answer is {expletive!}," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "This has been going on for years."

Trump followed up that post with more scathing remarks, taking shots at the network's ratings.

"Fox News Ratings are way down (27%!) because they're spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats!" he said. "All of those people who used to watch Fox, and no longer do, get it. It's them, not me — My numbers are better than they have ever been. The new CNN Poll stated that 'TRUMP' is at 99% among Republicans and, among Republican Presidents, 'TRUMP' is at 53%, compared to Ronald Reagan at 18%, and Abraham Lincoln at 8%! Fox knows this, and so does everyone else!"

"Also, why is Fox Corp. spending so much money donating to the Worst of the Worst, including Hakeem Jeffries, Jamie Raskin, Ted Lieu, Pete Aguilar, the California Dumocratic Party, the Dumocratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the Dumocratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, the Congressional Black Caucus PAC, the CHC Bold PAC, and the New Dumocrat Coalition Action Fund, among others? No wonder Fox News Ratings are collapsing, and they're going to go down a lot further. They're way down, not because of me, but because they are AGAINST me! This happened once before, and Fox almost collapsed. It's happening again!"

Trump slams Fox News host Jessica Tarlov over midterms coverage

Trump also targeted Fox News personality and "The Five" co-host Jessica Tarlov, calling her "DUMB AS A ROCK" and reportedly texting co-host Greg Gutfeld to complain about her.

Trump's relationship with Fox News has cooled considerably, despite the network's role in elevating his political profile through his appearances as a guest pundit on "Fox & Friends" and the praise he lavished on it during his first term.

Trump congratulates Democrats on midterm victory

Trump congratulated the Democrats on their midterm success on Tuesday, noting he's looking forward to working with them.

"My message is, congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country," he said in a phone call with CBS News.

"I know a lot of Democrats, I have total veto power and I'm sure we'll be able to work things out. I think they're gonna want to work with me. Otherwise I'd just veto everything and they're not gonna want that," he told the outlet.

NewsNation's Marty Hobe contributed to this report.

articles.title: Brown ousts Husted in battleground Ohio Senate race
articles.summary: (The Center Square) – Democrat Sherrod Brown is going back to the U. S.
articles.body:
(The Center Square) – Democrat Sherrod Brown is going back to the U.S. Senate, defeating U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, in a race that could decide control of the chamber.

Brown had 48.6% of the vote, with 87% of ballots tallied. The Associated Press called the race late Tuesday night.

The win marks a comeback for Brown, who lost reelection to U.S. Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, in 2024. He previously represented Ohio as a senator for 18 years between 2007 and 2025.

Husted was appointed to the Senate by Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine in January 2025 to replace Vice President JD Vance.

Tuesday's special election was a contest to fill the remainder of Vance's six-year Senate term, which he won in 2022. Brown will serve the final two years of Vance's term and would have to run for reelection in 2028 to win a full six-year term.

Senate Republicans went into the midterms with a tight 53-47 voting majority. To take back control of the chamber, Democrats needed to flip four seats while maintaining all the ones they currently hold.

Data centers emerged as a key issue for voters in Ohio's Senate race this election cycle.

The candidates' pitch to voters on the campaign trail centered on how to address the multibillion-dollar OpenAI data center project coming to southeastern Ohio. The project is set to be one of the largest data centers in the world.

Brown and Husted agreed that tech companies, not households, should be responsible for the power their data centers use, but they clashed on who is responsible for data center projects already underway.

In a campaign ad, Brown accused Husted of leading "the push to bring data centers to Ohio" and giving away "billions of tax dollars to make it happen." Husted said the decision to build data centers should belong to local communities.

Both candidates' campaigns focused on addressing inflation, an issue voters ranked as their top concern ahead of the midterms, according to polling by The Center Square .

Husted said tax cuts were the most effective way to bring costs down for consumers. He voted for the Republicans' 2025 tax and spending package, dubbed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, and touted it as "the largest tax cut in American history for middle-class families" in a campaign ad.

Brown criticized Republicans' economic legislation, saying the 2017 Trump tax cuts benefited wealthy taxpayers while leaving the middle class behind.

"All they've done is made things worse for Ohioans, handing over your hard-earned money to corporations and to billionaires," Brown said.

Brown raised more than triple that of Husted. Brown reported $68.4 million in total funds in his latest Federal Election Commission filings, while Husted reported $19.9 million.

articles.title: Democrats ride anti-Trump wave to win control of Congress
articles.summary: Democrats have captured both chambers of Congress, pushing deep into traditionally GOP territory to flip states and districts won by President Donald Trump.
articles.body:
Democrats have captured both chambers of Congress, pushing deep into traditionally GOP territory to flip states and districts won by President Donald Trump .

Decision Desk HQ and NBC projected Democrats would take the Senate, they had already been projected to win a majority in the House of Representatives earlier in the evening.

The results marked a stunning rebuke of the president, who barnstormed across the country in the final weeks of the campaign in a bid to keep red states in Republican hands. His efforts were unsuccessful as Democrats flipped Senate seats in South Carolina, North Carolina, Texas, Ohio, Kansas and Iowa.

Democrats needed to pick up four seats to take control of the chamber.

Midterm hopefuls vote and greet supporters

Adding to GOP woes, Democrats won several of the states by wide margins. Adam Hamilton is projected to be the first Democrat to win a Kansas Senate seat since 1932. James Talarico is the first Democrat to win a Texas Senate seat since 1988.

A competitive Senate race in Michigan, where Abdul El-Sayed is looking to keep the seat in Democratic hands remains uncalled.

Senate, Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-New York, called victory a "generational remake" of the Senate.

"We have five words for the American people," he said. "Relief is on the way."

Democrats had always been expected to flip the House, but the GOP entered 2026 favored to keep the Senate thanks to Democrats needing to flip at least three Senate seats in states Trump carried in 2024. But Trump's dipping popularity and skyrocketing cost of living radically altered that midterm outlook.

During the campaign, Democrats were relentless in winning over voters frustrated with the White House's failure to tame the economy. They also leaned heavily into allegations of corruption and enrichment by Trump and his allies since their return to power.

Retaking the Senate will give Democrats legislative leverage in terms of shaping Washington's agenda. They are likely to pursue reversing Medicaid and food stamp cuts; reasserting Congress' role on foreign trade policy; and seeking bipartisan agreement on banning lawmakers from trading stocks.

The immediate showdown, however, will likely center on the war in Iran, and could see Democrats directing Trump to seek congressional authorization to continue or pulling funding to end the conflict.

Trump also will have a harder time installing Cabinet and judicial nominees, including for another potential Supreme Court vacancy, should one arise.

More broadly, the wins give Democrats a jolt of energy heading into a presidential election year.

articles.title: Amy Acton wins Ohio race for governor, ending 16 years of Republican control of office
articles.summary: Democratic doctor wins over Vivek Ramaswamy, the biotech entrepreneur endorsed by Donald Trump
articles.body:
Democrat Amy Acton was elected governor of Ohio on Tuesday, after an ugly contest in which her rival Vivek Ramaswamy spent millions of dollars on deeply personal attack ads featuring her estranged mother.

Acton, 60, will become the first woman to serve as Ohio's governor, ending 16 years of Republican control.

In the final weeks leading up to election day, the race had become one of the most expensive and bitter in the country. Ramaswamy's campaign aired an ad that featured Acton's mother calling her a liar. Acton's mother lost custody of her after her husband, Acton's stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton when she was 12.

The spot drew backlash from politicians of both parties, who urged Ramaswamy to take it down and apologize. But Trump and JD Vance, the vice-president, backed Ramaswamy's minute-long ad, which the campaign said it would spend $4m on airing. The ad was eventually discontinued last week .

Acton, 60, led Ohio's health department through the first months of the Covid-19 pandemic. She will become the first woman to serve as Ohio's governor. Her defeat of Ramaswamy, the biotech entrepreneur endorsed by Trump, makes her the first Democrat to win the post since Ted Strickland in 2006. She succeeds Mike DeWine, the term-limited Republican.

Acton will lead a state that backed Trump by 11 points in 2024, and will govern alongside a Republican-controlled legislature, setting up potential clashes over tax reform, school funding and datacenters.

Ramaswamy won Trump's endorsement the day he launched his campaign, and promised voters he would revive the American Dream by making Ohio income-tax free in a decade, cutting energy bills, and restoring "law and order" to Ohio's cities.

Acton meanwhile centered her campaign on lowering costs, promising an earned income tax credit, a child tax credit of up to $1,000, a public prescription drug platform and property tax relief aimed at seniors and middle-income homeowners. She cast herself as a pragmatist, who had served in a Republican administration under DeWine.

The journey to election day was tumultuous for Acton, a first-time candidate who, like Ramaswamy, had never held elected office. Early polls showed her trailing by double digits, with roughly a quarter of voters saying they had never heard of her. For months, Democrats speculated that better-known figures, including former senator Sherrod Brown and former congressman Tim Ryan, might enter the race.

By mid-October, Ramaswamy and his allies had spent more than $100m on ads against Acton, roughly three times what her campaign spent, hammering her role in the state's pandemic shutdowns. At an October rally in Youngstown, Trump called Acton "a radical left lunatic".

But polling moved steadily in her direction through the fall, and a string of October polls showed her ahead until her eventual victory.

articles.title: 'I wasn't on the ballot': Trump distances himself from midterm results
articles.summary: "I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!" Trump wrote on social media.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump sought to distance himself from Republicans' mounting midterm losses Tuesday, declaring in his first remarks on the election results that his party would have been victorious had he been on the ballot.

"I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!" Trump wrote on social media.

Trump's efforts to sidestep blame for the growing blue wave came as Republicans were dealt stunning losses in deep red states and districts, with Democrats flipping Senate seats in Texas, South Carolina, Kansas and Ohio. Republicans also lost Senate races in North Carolina and Georgia, and are trailing in other key contests.

Trump told the New York Times that he is "absolutely willing to accept" the election results.

"We'll work with the Democrats, and we'll, you know, look forward to working with them. We'll probably work something out," Trump said.

Democrats are poised to flip both chambers of Congress by wide margins, with the party seizing on backlash to Trump's second-term agenda, including concerns about his handling of the economy and the Iran war.

Despite his record-low approval rating, Trump thrust himself into the center of the midterm election with a series of rallies across 20 states in the closing weeks.

The midterm contests are shaping up to be an emphatic repudiation of a president who implored voters to "pretend" he was on the ballot.

articles.title: Democrats sweep Texas
articles.summary: Republicans ran the country's second most-populous state for 30 years. Tonight Democrats took it back.
articles.body:
AUSTIN — Democrats' vision of a blue Texas is finally here.

James Talarico has been elected a U.S. senator and Gina Hinojosa as governor, the first Democrats to win either office in more than a generation. The four other statewide candidates are leading as ballots continue to be counted. Democrats further down the ballot are leading some red districts, changing the complexion of the state legislature, congressional delegation and courts.

"It's something that I haven't seen in decades, that none of us have seen in decades," said former Texas House Speaker Joe Straus, a moderate Republican.

It's an outcome that even the most bullish Democrats didn't dare enunciate in the late days of the election. But as results have poured in Tuesday night, the party is outpacing its expectations across the country's second most populous state amidst a national romp.

Both Hinojosa's and Talarico's victory margins came by running up vote counts in Texas' deep-blue urban centers and while also leading in the largest Republican-led county in the country, Tarrant County. They reversed Republican gains across the Latino-heavy Rio Grande Valley region, an ancestrally Democratic area that had swung hard to the right in recent years. Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez romped to a near-20 point victory in a seat Republicans drew to favor them during last year's redrawing of the state's House map, ousting a top Republican recruit who campaigned alongside Speaker Mike Johnson to begin election day.

"I've been around for a long time, and I've never seen a shift [like this]," said Democratic Rep. Henry Cuellar, who is on track to win his newly redrawn South Texas seat by over 30 points. "When Trump did well in South Texas, they said things had shifted. It was not a political realignment. What we're seeing today is a political realignment."

It amounts to a set of remarkable results in a state that hasn't elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1988 and to the governor's mansion since 1990. In recent cycles, Democrats have tried and failed to flip the state in presidential and U.S. Senate contests but have been largely uncompetitive for state offices. But Tuesday's blue wave slammed into Texas particularly hard, as it combined frustrations over the economy, immigration enforcement, data centers and corruption with a collapse of Trump's 2024 coalition.

"We reminded voters that Republicans have been in charge in Texas for 30 years. That every problem we have, was caused by Republicans," Michelle Lowe Solis, chair of the Bexar County Democratic Party. "They aren't going to fix the problems, they caused them."

As votes continue to be counted, Democrats appear poised to blunt the impact of Republicans' attempted gerrymander, likely sweeping the Rio Grande Valley congressional seats while holding onto another San Antonio-area district drawn to favor Republicans. In state Supreme Court races, they lead in all four seats up for grabs, potentially turning a 9-0 conservative majority into a 5-4 split. Among the first 36 state house races called by the Associated Press, 34 have gone to Democrats and just two to Republicans."Voters aren't dumb," said Rep. Linda Sanchez (D-Calif.), who chairs the Congressional Hispanic Caucus' BOLD PAC. "Even though the Republicans have tried to cheat with the series of gerrymanders, that has, I think, only made voters in those areas more willing to participate."

Talarico's and Hinojosa's victories will be felt nationally. Texas Democrats, who have long asked for national money and resources in a state where elections are costly, now have a test case of how to win. And it will bolster their arguments that their state, with 40 electoral votes, should be treated as a presidential battleground.

"This is something I've been working on for the last two decades," said Gonzalez. "Today is a dream fulfilled for a lot of people and a new dawn in Texas."

Ali Bianco and Jonathan Martin contributed reporting.
