articles.title: Democrat Josh Turek wins Iowa Senate race
articles.summary: Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek defeated GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson in the Iowa Senate race, CBS News projects, in a major pickup for Democrats as they seek to...
articles.body:
Washington — Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek defeated GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson in the Iowa Senate race, CBS News projects, in a major pickup for Democrats as they seek to take control of the upper chamber.

Turek, 47, is a former wheelchair basketball Paralympian and state representative who campaigned on his record of working across the aisle, and sought what was initially viewed as a long-shot bid for the seat in the U.S Senate after GOP Sen. Joni Ernst announced she wouldn't seek reelection.

But the race proved more competitive than expected, despite the state's rightward shift in recent years, as the Trump administration's trade policies, the unpopular war in Iran and high gas and diesel prices hit Iowans especially hard.

Hinson, 43, is a former local news anchor who has represented Iowa in the House since 2021 and initially vowed to be President Trump's "top ally" in the Senate. Hinson had to tread a fine line as she pitched her candidacy in the Hawkeye State. In the weeks ahead of the election, Hinson called for the war to be brought to a "successful and immediate end," though she had opposed efforts in Congress to rein in the president's war powers. And during a debate in October, while she said she'll be the president's ally when it's "important for Iowa," she also pledged to "push back on him."

In the leadup to election day, polls showed Hinson and Turek locked in a tight race, forcing both sides to spend heavily in the state.

Once a swing state, Iowa hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008, and Mr. Trump won the state by 13 points in 2024.

The projected victory brought Democrats a fifth flip, giving them enough seats to secure a majority. Despite a map that had initially looked favorable to Republicans, steep headwinds emerged for the party as competitive races cropped up in reliably red states like Iowa in recent months, throwing the GOP's hold on the upper chamber into question.

Democrat Rob Sand won the governor's race in Iowa.

articles.title: Michigan U.S. Senate race between El-Sayed, Rogers too close to call
articles.summary: (The Center Square) – The Michigan U. S.
articles.body:
(The Center Square) – The Michigan U.S. Senate race between progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers is too close to call, with votes still being counted in one of the nation's most closely watched contests.

El-Sayed and Rogers remain locked in a tight contest. Michigan has not elected a Republican to the U.S. Senate since 1994, and Rogers also lost his bid for the seat in 2024.

With 48% of precincts reporting at midnight, El-Sayed was leading 50.3%-47.8%, with more than 2.4 million votes counted.

The winner will succeed Democratic U.S. Sen. Gary Peters, who was first elected in 2014. Peters announced in January 2025 that he would not seek reelection.

The race between El-Sayed and Rogers was particularly heated and was considered one of the nation's most consequential U.S. Senate contests, with control of the 120th Congress hanging in the balance.

Democrats were divided during the primary between El-Sayed and establishment-backed U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens. El-Sayed, who is seeking to become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, narrowly defeated Stevens.

Following the primary, much of the Democratic establishment rallied behind the 41-year-old El-Sayed. Former President Barack Obama campaigned alongside him in Detroit. However, Stevens broke with her party's nominee, endorsing Rogers in the final days of the campaign.

Going into election night, El-Sayed was leading Rogers in the polls by upwards of 6%, generally outside the margin of error.

In 2024, Michigan's U.S. Senate race was decided by less than half a percentage point, with Democrat Elissa Slotkin narrowly defeating Rogers. Rogers returned as the Republican nominee in 2026 after securing the party's nomination unopposed.

El-Sayed is seeking to become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. He has cast himself as a progressive and faced repeated allegations of extremism throughout his campaign. During a weekend rally, Trump called him a "jihadist" and said he was "on the side of the terrorists."

The 41-year-old responded to the president's frequent attacks on the campaign trail.

"I don't even care that he remembers my whole name because he can just go on and call me 'senator' after November," El-Sayed said during a rally Sunday. "I will be Senator Muhammad to you, bro."

articles.title: Democrat Annie Andrews wins South Carolina Senate race
articles.summary: Democrat Annie Andrews won a stunning upset over GOP Sen. Darline Graham, who was running for her late brother Lindsey Graham's seat.
articles.body:
Washington — Democrat Annie Andrews defeated GOP Sen. Darline Graham in the South Carolina Senate race, CBS News projects, in a major upset.

Andrews, 45, is a pediatrician and campaigned on healthcare access and affordability, along with fighting corruption in Washington. She faced off against Graham, the incumbent senator who was appointed to serve out the remainder of her brother Lindsey Graham's term after his sudden death in July.

Darline Graham, 62, most recently served as commissioner of the South Carolina Commission for the Blind, before she was appointed to the Senate. She went on to win a special primary election to take her brother's place on the ballot to represent South Carolina for a full six-year term.

Andrews faced an uphill battle in a state that hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1998, and which President Trump won by 18 points in 2024. She criticized Darline Graham for lacking experience, pointing to comments she made during the condensed primary, when she said she was "not that informed on national security."

The race, which grew much more competitive than expected, forced Republicans to come to Graham's aid with a $5 million investment in October from the Senate Leadership Fund, the main Republican super PAC. MAGA Inc., a super PAC controlled by Mr. Trump, also gave Graham $827,000 in August, and he personally campaigned heavily for Graham after encouraging her to run for the seat. But the efforts fell short amid a difficult environment for Republicans.

With Andrews' projected victory, Democrats secured an unexpected pickup, helping to propel them to a majority.

articles.title: ‘Buckle up’: A defiant White House pins blame elsewhere
articles.summary: Tonight’s elections are a repudiation of Republicans that some in the White House have been unwilling to own.
articles.body:
The White House began Tuesday night with cautious optimism. As Democrats started racking up victories, President Donald Trump's advisers grew more candid — and defiant.

Trump spent the weeks before the midterms traveling across the country, hosting 30 events across 20 states in just over a month as he urged voters to "pretend that I'm on the ballot." What resulted was a midterm repudiation of Republicans that, as election night wore on, some in the White House were unwilling to own.

"President Trump was not on the ballot, and it's proven that Trump voters show up when he is on the ballot," a White House official told Semafor, arguing that he "did a better job promoting many of the candidates on the ballot than the candidates did themselves."

Trump himself echoed the sentiment in a Tuesday night social media post : "I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!"

The early results on Tuesday night made clear that Trump's aggressive campaign push wasn't enough to surmount public frustration with the Iran war and his tariffs' effect on the cost of living. Democrats quickly flipped North Carolina, held onto New Hampshire and Georgia — and then flipped long-scarlet South Carolina. Trump officials and people close to the White House quickly acknowledged that a massive blue wave was coming.

One Trump administration official emphasized how much the war has directly affected Americans. That conflict amplified voters' frustration as gas prices climbed, and many in Trump's base felt betrayed by a president who'd campaigned on launching no new wars.

Another Trump ally went even further, describing the war as a "disaster" and lamenting that "the Republican party doesn't understand the Trump coalition, even though it's 10 years in."

Officials' efforts to pin their stunning midterm setback on other GOP leaders suggest that the White House has no plans to seek conciliation with ascendant congressional Democratic majorities.

"Regardless of how today plays out, President Trump's resolve to stop the Radical Left is only going to become stronger," the White House official added. "Buckle up."

Trump told The New York Times late Tuesday that he would accept the results of the election.

In the past few weeks, some administration officials have begun looking to hire lawyers to preempt Democrat-led investigations — an early sign that they knew Tuesday night's results might not go their way. To that point, some advisers indicated to Semafor that the results rolling in so far were not surprising to them. Trump has often pointed over the past months to historical data showing that the party holding total control of Washington tends to perform poorly in midterm elections.

Even before polls across the country closed, the White House began circulating talking points highlighting Trump's efforts on the trail. That underlying message — that the president did what he could to help — largely persisted inside the administration as the losses mounted. One adviser told Semafor that Trump's thinking remains along those lines: that he did what he could.

Several Trump allies also argued to Semafor that poor candidate quality was partly to blame for Republican defeats, though the president openly endorsed several of the candidates who fell short.

Trump certainly made himself a central figure in Tuesday's election. Democrats looked to amplify his calls for voters to pretend he was on the ballot, believing that voters were so dissatisfied with the administration that a midterm referendum on Trump would reward them.

Trump watched the election results roll in from the White House East Room alongside Cabinet members, senior staff, and political advisers, another White House official told Semafor. At times, he took to Truth Social to rage against Fox News' coverage of the evening.

Some staffers ordered in from the Cheesecake Factory, an apparent nod to the now-famous quip from former President Barack Obama about Trump's decorating.

Tonight's results are a warning sign for the Republican Party as it tries to look past Trump. And they're likely to surface a question that some of his aides knew they'd inevitably face: whether the coalition that pushed Trump to power can be reconstituted, and what the party will stand for after Trump leaves office.

Some Republicans I've texted with tonight are already confronting that question. In the weeks and months ahead, anyone in the GOP who's eyeing a 2028 run will need to look at the midterm results and find ways to run with a different message than Trump — while not angering him or his base.

articles.title: Troy Jackson defeats Susan Collins to flip Maine Senate seat for Dems
articles.summary: Democrat Troy Jackson has defeated Susan Collins, a five-term incumbent and the last Republican senator left in New England.
articles.body:
Democrat Troy Jackson has defeated Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, flipping a long Republican-held seat and giving his party a crucial win as they seek to flip the U.S. Senate, according to projections by CNN and Fox News .

Collins called her opponent to concede, Jackson campaign spokesperson Maggie Amjad confirmed to USA TODAY.

Jackson had just a few months to run his Senate campaign after oyster farmer Graham Platner dropped out of the race following accusations of sexual assault, which he denies. Platner's charisma and anti-establishment messaging had inspired a grassroots movement that helped him overtake Maine's Democratic Gov. Janet Mills in the Democratic primary.

Platner's exit from the race prompted worries about the Democrats' chances of defeating Collins, who has been in office for 30 years and is the only Republican to represent a state won by Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. The race remained in a dead heat through much of the year, according to polls.

But many remained committed to the movement and Jackson, a logger who served as state Senate president for six years, was also seen as an ideologically similar champion for economic populist policies—if less charismatic and sometimes emotional . While he started his career as a Republican who opposed abortion and gay marriage, he is now a progressive Democrat who has received high scores from abortion and LGBTQ groups . As a state legislator, he cosponsored Maine's expanded abortion rights protection and passed legislation giving loggers and haulers the right to unionize .

Throughout the campaign, Jackson highlighted his progressive bonafides, campaigning with heavy weights like Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Verment, and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-New York, while tying Collins to President Donald Trump .

Collins has long held a reputation as a moderate Republican who has brought a lot of money back for Maine, and those are the arguments she leaned on in her campaign. But that reputation has been harder to uphold in the Trump era, where Mainers increasingly saw her as not doing enough to stop Trump's agenda. According to an October Marist poll , 59% of Maine voters disapproved of the president.

See Susan Collins, Troy Jackson and more campaign in Maine midterms

An Oct. 1 analysis of the majority of Trump's second term from CQ Roll Call found Collins voted with the president 92% of the time. A New York Times analysis of her voting record found that her opposing votes rarely stopped Trump's agenda from passing. In one debate where Collins was asked for an example in which she voted against her party and actually changed the outcome, she touted her vote against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth – but Hegseth was ultimately confirmed.

In an interview before the election, University of Maine Farmington political science professor Jim Melcher told USA TODAY that Trump, in some ways, has been "the absolute worst thing that could have happened to Susan Collins."

articles.title: Jon Ossoff wins Georgia Senate race, keeping seat for Democrats
articles.summary: Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff defeated GOP Rep. Mike Collins in the Georgia Senate race, CBS News projects, holding onto his seat in the upper chamber.
articles.body:
Washington — Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff defeated GOP Rep. Mike Collins in the Georgia Senate race, CBS News projects, holding onto his seat in the upper chamber.

Ossoff, 39, was the sole Democrat seeking reelection in a state that President Trump won in 2024. He first came to the Senate in 2021, when he delivered Democrats one of two runoff victories in Georgia. This cycle, Republicans saw the race as a key prize as they sought to keep control of the chamber. But after a messy primary fight, and facing personal controversies and national headwinds, Collins was unable to make significant inroads in the Peach State.

Collins, 59, prevailed during the primary, becoming the Republican nominee in June after a runoff. The owner of a trucking business, Collins has represented Georgia in the House since 2023, and attempted to cast Ossoff as out of touch with Georgian values. But his campaign was beset by questions about people in Collins' circle, including a former staffer who reportedly shared Nazi and KKK images on social media.

Although the race was once viewed as the easiest pickup opportunity for Republicans, as Georgia shifted toward the right during the last election, Collins' closeness to the president was seen as a boon for Ossoff, who has also been a formidable fundraiser. Heading into election night, Ossoff was leading in the polls.

With the projected victory, Democrats retained a key seat, helping to cement their majority.

articles.title: Science is moving beyond animal testing. Why is India going backwards?
articles.summary: Using animal biology to model human disease has long reached its scientific and moral limits.
articles.body: Using animal biology to model human disease has long reached its scientific and moral limits. Worldwide, progressive regulators are replacing animal experimentation with human-relevant methods that deliver faster, more reliable safety data. But India is poised to weaken statutory protections and lower ethical standards it has, ironically, demonstrated leadership in.At the centre of this regressive shift is the draft Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (Control and Supervision of Experiments, Breeding and Trading of Laboratory Animals) Rules 2026. Issued by Committee for Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals (CCSEA) under fisheries, animal husbandry and dairying ministry, the proposed text seeks to replace foundational frameworks established in 1968 and 1998.

articles.title: Lone Star turns blue: Democrats Talarico, Hinojosa topple Texas Republicans
articles.summary: Democrat James Talarico, a former schoolteacher and Presbyterian seminarian who campaigned on a "politics of love," on Tuesday won the US Senate race in Texa...
articles.body:
Democrat James Talarico, a former schoolteacher and Presbyterian seminarian who campaigned on a "politics of love," on Tuesday won the US Senate race in Texas, dealing a historic blow to Republicans that could reshape American politics.

Talarico defeated the state's attorney general Ken Paxton, a close ally of President Donald Trump who was heavily backed by tech billionaire Elon Musk, US media projected.

The result was a major setback for Trump, who threw his weight behind Paxton and made the state a campaign priority.

"We defeated Goliath," Talarico told a victory rally in Austin, the state capital.

"In this race, we went up against our own Goliaths. The richest man in the world, the most powerful man in the world, and the entire Washington, DC establishment," he said.

Talarico took aim at billionaires "who own the social media algorithms, who own the cable news networks, who own the politicians fighting on our screens" and who "want us at each other's throats."

In another political earthquake for the deeply conservative southern border state, Democrat Gina Hinojosa unseated incumbent Texas Governor Greg Abbott.

Talarico and Hinojosa are the first Democrats to win statewide office in Texas since 1994.

Hinojosa, a 52-year-old attorney and state lawmaker, is part of a new generation of Democrats who are seeking to attract independents and voters disillusioned by Trump's unpopular war in the Middle East and skyrocketing prices for gas and everyday goods.

Thousands of supporters gathered at a watch party in Austin erupted in joy as the results came in, many of them crying and hugging.

Some chanted "Si se puede" ("Yes we can" in Spanish), while drivers passing by honked their horns in celebration.

"It's a huge win for Texas, but it's a giant win for the United States, having James Talarico in the Senate to try to wrest control of this government that's out of control," said Kathy Jackoway, an Austin resident in her 60s.

"Everybody is suffering. Everybody is hurting, and Trump is busy building monuments to himself."

Anisha, 29, said she hoped the two Democrats would govern "for everyone, not just the billionaires, not just the elite."

The landmark victories for Democrats could signal that Texas, the country's second most populous state with 40 electoral votes, is becoming competitive in national elections, a shift that could reshape the electoral map for future races.

"This is a win the size of Texas and now we have a mandate the size of Texas," Talarico said.

The results mark a bruising defeat for Musk, who spent more than $200 million to support Talarico's rival, according to federal filings.

The world's richest man, Musk has moved the headquarters of Tesla, SpaceX and X to Texas.

The spread of AI data centers across Texas became a central issue in both races, as residents worried about rising electricity bills, water use and strain on the power grid.

Talarico and Hinojosa both called for tighter regulation, prompting Abbott, a longtime champion of the industry, to propose new rules of his own.

Talarico ran on a blend of Christian faith and economic populism, describing the contest as a David versus Goliath fight and inviting Republicans dissatisfied with the party to join him.

Trump traveled to Texas four times in the month before the election to rally for Paxton, whom he endorsed over four-term incumbent senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary.

Talarico, 37, was elected to the Texas House of Representatives in 2018 and built a national following with speeches combining progressive politics, biblical teaching and criticism of wealthy elites.

He defeated congresswoman Jasmine Crockett in the Democratic primary and sought to broaden his appeal by criticizing aspects of former president Joe Biden's immigration policies.

Paxton, 63, survived impeachment by the Republican-controlled Texas House in 2023 on allegations of corruption and abuse of power before being acquitted by the state Senate. He has denied wrongdoing.

During the campaign, Talarico drew support from voters who had left the Republican Party, as well as from younger voters.
